newsitem.title: FRANCE: Framatome merger talks fail on power stakes.
newsitem.headline: Framatome merger talks fail on power stakes.

text.p: French state-controlled nuclear engineering group Framatome said on Monday that a planned merger with GEC-Alsthom seemed unlikely to be achieved.
It said that the General Electric Company Plc had wanted to have a stake of 50 percent in the new combination, equal to its current stake in the GEC Alsthom joint-venture with Alcatel Alsthom.
But this wish went against the government's condition that French interests keep a majority in the nuclear group.
In a statement, Framatome said its supervisory board had met on April 4 and had underlined the strategic interest in the medium and long term of an alliance, both for Framatome and GEC Alsthom.

It said that the main shareholders of Framatome had told the board that "the completion of the merger in line with the original conditions was unlikely and that they continued to explore the conditions in which the sought after industrial synergies can be obtained in a manner acceptable to all".
Framatome is 44 percent owned by Alcatel Alsthom. The rest is held by state-owned groups CEA Industrie, Electricite de France (EDF) and the Consortium de Realisation (CDR).

Alcatel chairman Serge Tchuruk said on March 18 that the talks about a merger between Framatome anmd GEC Alsthom had run into difficulties and he added that Alcatel and GEC were now in talks about wider cooperation than the GEC Alsthom venture for industrial power and high speed trains.

Industry Minister Franck Borotra last year imposed five conditions for the state agreeing to the merger. They included France keeping control over its nuclear destiny and Framatome continuing work with Siemens AG on a new reactor.
Borotra on Friday invited GEC to start talks with either Alcatel or Lagardere Group about joining a bid for the state's 58 percent stake in defence electronics group Thomson-CSF.
Earlier that day, the government had rejected GEC's stand-alone bid for Thomson-CSF, citing national security considerations.
